sections.title: Intermediate Introduction to Counting Figures
sections.content: At this level, figures become more complex. Multiple lines intersect each other, creating hidden shapes. Questions may include overlapped triangles, star polygons, irregular grids, and 3D projection figures. To reach the correct answer, shapes must be counted systematically from smallest to largest.

sections.title: Counting Overlapping Triangles
sections.content: When several triangles overlap each other, first identify the smallest triangles. Then count the medium triangles formed by combining two smaller ones. Finally, count the larger triangles formed by the entire structure. In some figures, a hexagonal center may appear, which creates additional triangles.

sections.title: Figures in Star Polygons
sections.content: In star-shaped figures, multiple diagonal lines form small triangles and quadrilaterals. First count the outer small triangles. Then count the triangles and quadrilaterals formed around the center. Finally, count the large shapes formed by the complete figure.

sections.title: Squares and Rectangles in Irregular Grids
sections.content: Sometimes the grid is not perfectly symmetrical. In such cases, first count all possible small squares. Then count larger squares and rectangles formed by combining two or more blocks. Remember that any closed region formed by four corners can create a square or rectangle.

sections.title: Counting Cubes in 3D Projection
sections.content: Some figures appear as 3D cube structures. In such questions, visible cubes, partially hidden cubes, and cubes forming the entire structure must be counted separately. It is useful to visualize the structure in layers such as front layer, middle layer, and back layer.

sections.title: Identifying Hidden Figures
sections.content: In complex diagrams, many shapes are not directly visible. To identify them, observe the intersection points of lines and mentally connect them to form possible shapes. Diagonal lines often create extra shapes that students commonly overlook.

sections.title: 3–4 Step Counting Process
sections.content: Step 1: Identify the smallest triangles, squares, or rectangles. Step 2: Count medium shapes formed by combining two or more smaller parts. Step 3: Count large shapes formed by the entire structure. Step 4: Check for hidden diagonal or composite shapes.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content: Failing to notice hidden shapes, counting only straight shapes while ignoring diagonal ones, overlooking large shapes, and counting the same shape more than once.

sections.title: Quick Summary
sections.content: In intermediate-level Counting Figures, systematic counting is essential. Start with smaller shapes, then combined shapes, and finally the largest shapes. Pay special attention to diagonal lines and hidden shapes formed in the center.

tricks.title: Overlapping Triangle Identification
tricks.explanation: Where several lines meet in one region, both small and large triangles are formed. Count the smallest ones first, then the combined triangles.
tricks.example: In a figure with three overlapping triangles, count the small triangles, combinations of two, and the full triangle.

tricks.title: Hexagon Center Trick
tricks.explanation: If the center of the figure forms a hexagon-like shape, many hidden triangles are usually formed around it.
tricks.example: Six lines meeting in the center may create a hexagon surrounded by multiple small triangles.

tricks.title: Star Shape Counting
tricks.explanation: In star shapes, start by counting triangles at the outer points, then count the combined triangles at the center.
tricks.example: In a 5-point star, count the 5 outer triangles first and then the inner triangles.

tricks.title: Irregular Grid Strategy
tricks.explanation: If the grid is uneven, examine every possible four-corner combination to identify rectangles.
tricks.example: In a 3x2 grid, count small rectangles, vertical rectangles, and the full-grid rectangle.

tricks.title: 3D Cube Layer Method
tricks.explanation: Visualize cubes in layers such as front, top, and back to avoid missing hidden cubes.
tricks.example: A cube structure may show 4 cubes in front and 2 cubes on top.

tricks.title: Check Diagonal Lines
tricks.explanation: Diagonal lines often create extra triangles that students forget to count.
tricks.example: A square with two diagonals forms several additional triangles.

tricks.title: Center-Out Counting
tricks.explanation: Start counting shapes near the center and then move outward.
tricks.example: In a star figure, count the central triangles before the outer ones.

tricks.title: Composite Shape Identification
tricks.explanation: Two or more small shapes can combine to form a larger one.
tricks.example: Two small triangles can combine to form one larger triangle.

tricks.title: Intersection Point Method
tricks.explanation: Where lines intersect, new corners are formed which can create additional shapes.
tricks.example: Four intersecting lines may produce several small triangles.

tricks.title: Count the Entire Figure Last
tricks.explanation: The entire figure itself often forms the largest shape that must be counted.
tricks.example: Among many small squares, the complete outer square also counts as one.
